summary:
West Java stands under the national framework of Indonesia, which is a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment; because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, that provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations, and reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

Sub-national variation sits inside that framework. Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women alongside national-level morality provisions, and in Aceh two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025. Those provincial provisions apply to foreign visitors present in those provinces, not to West Java; West Java's own exposure comes from national law, national police action and street violence.

Police in West Java investigate and break up LGBT gatherings even where no offence is alleged. On 22 June 2025 the West Java Regional Police confirmed the detention of 75 people, 74 men and one woman, at a privately rented villa in Puncak in Bogor Regency, following a tip from local residents; police described the event as an LGBT family gathering held to avoid detection. Amnesty International, which said the gathering violated no law, called the operation a discriminatory raid and a blatant violation of human rights and privacy and demanded release and accountability.

Street violence against trans women is documented in the province. On 15 August 2026 reporting from Bogor recorded men dousing a trans woman on a public street with what appeared to be urine, one of a wave of attacks. Activists tied the violence to a 2025 presidential regulation classifying the spread of LGBTQ culture as a non-military threat and to discriminatory regional regulations, arguing that official language legitimises violence against trans women; a trans woman quoted in the report said that people who previously appeared in public now live in fear.
tangentialFactors:
Hostility in West Java is reinforced by the national regulatory backdrop. A presidential decree of October 2025 lists LGBTQ+ people as a non-military national threat alongside separatism and terrorism, placing them within national defence policy, and reporting in August 2026 links the surge in vigilante attacks on trans people directly to that decree and to officials' public condemnations.

Expression is criminalised in ways a visitor can trigger. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction punishes any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment; the national broadcasting commission banned television and radio programmes presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal in March 2016, the government has blocked websites and apps carrying gay or LGBTQ-related words including Grindr, and a bill to prohibit online content presenting LGBT behaviour was under discussion in 2025.

Custody has proved lethal. In August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges and died in custody; his mother alleges police beat him and says authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release, while Indonesian police deny that violence was used.

National-level raids continue beyond West Java, and police have acted on gatherings elsewhere in the country on the same pattern seen at Puncak.
localsOnly:
Indonesia recognises only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors, with no third-gender or X option, and legal gender recognition requires sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval. No national law protects people from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.

Residents of West Java live under both the national framework and provincial regulations. Activists cited in August 2026 reporting identify discriminatory regional regulations in the province as one driver of the attacks on trans women, alongside the 2025 presidential regulation on the spread of LGBTQ culture.

West Java Regional Police confirmed the Puncak arrests, indicating that detentions of LGBT gatherings are an established investigative practice by the provincial police command rather than an isolated unit's action.
outOfScopeNotes:
The specific West Java regional regulations described as discriminatory are not named or cited in the source material, and their content and penalties are unresolved.

Whether any of the 75 people detained at Puncak on 22 June 2025 were subsequently charged, and with what offence, is not sourced here; Amnesty International stated that the gathering violated no law and called for release, and no charging outcome is recorded.

The number of attacks in the wave reported around 15 August 2026, and whether any arrests or prosecutions followed the Bogor assault, are not established by the sources.

The West Java profile does not address entry screening, visa refusal on gender-identity grounds, or access to gender-affirming care for visitors; those questions are not resolved at this level and must be assessed against the national record.
